claim: V1 ChCs predominantly receive monosynaptic input from local layer 5 pyramidal cells.
source: Using viral tracing we found that V1 ChCs predominantly receive monosynaptic input from local layer 5 pyramidal cells and higher-order cortical regions.
evidence: The claim is supported by retrograde rabies tracing experiments showing that most labeled neurons providing input to ChCs were located in L5 of V1, as shown in Figure 1C and described in the Results section.

claim: V1 ChCs receive monosynaptic input from higher-order cortical regions.
source: Using viral tracing we found that V1 ChCs predominantly receive monosynaptic input from local layer 5 pyramidal cells and higher-order cortical regions.
evidence: The claim is supported by retrograde rabies tracing experiments showing labeled neurons in various cortical regions including RSC and S1, as shown in Figure 1B-C. Optogenetic experiments confirmed monosynaptic connections from RSC (Figure 1H).

claim: ChCs are visually responsive but weakly selective for stimulus content.
source: Two-photon calcium imaging and convolutional neural network modeling revealed that ChCs are visually responsive but weakly selective for stimulus content.
evidence: The claim is supported by two-photon calcium imaging showing ChCs respond to visual stimuli (Figure 2D-E, Figure 3B) and CNN modeling showing they have lower sparsity and orientation selectivity than PyCs (Figure 3C, G).

claim: ChCs respond strongly to locomotion.
source: In mice running in a virtual tunnel, ChCs respond strongly to events known to elicit arousal, including locomotion and visuomotor mismatch.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data showing ChCs are highly correlated with running speed (Figure 2C) and show strong responses at locomotion onset (Figure 4F, J).

claim: ChCs respond strongly to visuomotor mismatch.
source: In mice running in a virtual tunnel, ChCs respond strongly to events known to elicit arousal, including locomotion and visuomotor mismatch.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data showing ChCs have strong responses when visual flow is halted during running (Figure 4E, I).

claim: Repeated exposure of mice to the virtual tunnel was accompanied by reduced visual responses of ChCs.
source: Repeated exposure of the mice to the virtual tunnel was accompanied by reduced visual responses of ChCs and structural plasticity of ChC boutons and axon initial segment length.
evidence: The claim is supported by chronic imaging experiments showing ChCs had significantly reduced responses to moving gratings after training in the virtual tunnel (Figure 5B-D).

claim: Repeated exposure of mice to the virtual tunnel was accompanied by structural plasticity of ChC boutons.
source: Repeated exposure of the mice to the virtual tunnel was accompanied by reduced visual responses of ChCs and structural plasticity of ChC boutons and axon initial segment length.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry showing increased fraction of AISs contacted by ChC boutons and increased bouton density after training (Figure 6D, G).

claim: Repeated exposure of mice to the virtual tunnel was accompanied by structural plasticity of axon initial segment length.
source: Repeated exposure of the mice to the virtual tunnel was accompanied by reduced visual responses of ChCs and structural plasticity of ChC boutons and axon initial segment length.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry showing decreased AIS length in trained mice compared to naive mice (Figure 6E-F).

claim: ChCs only weakly inhibited pyramidal cells.
source: Finally, ChCs only weakly inhibited pyramidal cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by chemogenetic silencing experiments showing only mild increases in PyC activity when ChCs were inhibited, with only 21% of PyCs showing significantly increased activity (Figure 7B, F).

claim: ChCs provide an arousal-related signal to layer 2/3 pyramidal cells.
source: These findings suggest that ChCs provide an arousal-related signal to layer 2/3 pyramidal cells that may modulate their activity and/or gate plasticity of their axon initial segments during behaviorally relevant events.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple observations: ChCs are highly correlated with arousal markers (pupil size, running speed, Figure 2C), respond to visuomotor mismatch (Figure 4E), and innervate L2/3 PyC AISs (Figure 1K, Figure 6).

claim: ChCs may modulate pyramidal cell activity during behaviorally relevant events.
source: These findings suggest that ChCs provide an arousal-related signal to layer 2/3 pyramidal cells that may modulate their activity and/or gate plasticity of their axon initial segments during behaviorally relevant events.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observation that ChCs respond to arousal-related events and weakly inhibit PyCs (Figure 7).

claim: ChCs may gate plasticity of pyramidal cell axon initial segments during behaviorally relevant events.
source: These findings suggest that ChCs provide an arousal-related signal to layer 2/3 pyramidal cells that may modulate their activity and/or gate plasticity of their axon initial segments during behaviorally relevant events.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observation that ChC innervation and AIS length change with experience (Figure 6) and ChCs respond to behaviorally relevant events (Figure 4).

claim: 87% of labeled neurons in Vipr2-Cre mice were ChCs based on morphological properties.
source: Quantification based on morphological properties (eYFP+ cell bodies at the L1/L2 border and L1 dendrites) revealed that 87% (287/329) of labeled neurons were ChCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological analysis of eYFP-labeled neurons in Vipr2-Cre mice showing characteristic ChC features (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).

claim: ChCs received long-range inputs from various thalamic and cortical regions including dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus, lateral posterior nucleus, retrosplenial cortex, and S1.
source: This revealed that ChCs received long-range inputs from various thalamic and cortical regions (e.g. dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus, lateral posterior nucleus, retrosplenial cortex, and S1), matching long-range inputs described for other interneuron subsets in V1 (Ma et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by rabies tracing experiments showing labeled neurons in these regions (Figure 1B-C) and is consistent with previous literature on V1 interneuron inputs.

claim: The most abundant sources of presynaptic partners of ChCs were found locally in L5 and to a lesser extent in L1–4 of V1.
source: The most abundant sources of presynaptic partners of ChCs, however, were found locally in L5 and to a lesser extent in L1–4 of V1 (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of rabies-labeled neurons showing the highest percentage of inputs from V1 L5 (Figure 1C).

claim: Labeled L5 neurons had pyramidal-shaped cell bodies and dendritic spines, indicating that L5 inputs to ChCs are excitatory.
source: Labeled L5 neurons had pyramidal-shaped cell bodies and dendritic spines, indicating that L5 inputs to ChCs are excitatory (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: The claim is based on morphological analysis of rabies-labeled L5 neurons showing pyramidal morphology and spines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-F), which are characteristic features of excitatory neurons.

claim: The local innervation pattern of V1 ChCs is reminiscent of ChCs in S1.
source: This local innervation pattern is reminiscent of ChCs in S1 (Xu and Callaway, 2009), but differs significantly from the innervation pattern of ChCs in the prefrontal cortex where they predominantly receive input from contralaterally projecting PyCs in deep layer 3 (Lu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with published literature on ChC connectivity in S1 and prefrontal cortex.

claim: The innervation pattern of V1 ChCs differs significantly from the innervation pattern of ChCs in the prefrontal cortex where they predominantly receive input from contralaterally projecting PyCs in deep layer 3.
source: This local innervation pattern is reminiscent of ChCs in S1 (Xu and Callaway, 2009), but differs significantly from the innervation pattern of ChCs in the prefrontal cortex where they predominantly receive input from contralaterally projecting PyCs in deep layer 3 (Lu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with published literature on ChC connectivity in prefrontal cortex.

claim: Local optogenetic activation of RSC boutons in V1 generated inward currents in ~85% (11/13) of voltage-clamped ChCs.
source: Local optogenetic activation of RSC boutons in V1 generated inward currents in ~85% (11/13) of voltage-clamped ChCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings showing optogenetically-evoked currents in ChCs (Figure 1G).

claim: The resulting excitatory postsynaptic potentials (PSPs) from RSC inputs were abolished in the presence of tetrodotoxin (TTX), but reappeared upon additional application of the potassium-channel blocker 4-aminopyridine (4-AP).
source: The resulting excitatory postsynaptic potentials (PSPs) were abolished in the presence of tetrodotoxin (TTX), but reappeared upon additional application of the potassium-channel blocker 4-aminopyridine (4-AP) (Figure 1H), which facilitates optogenetically evoked synaptic release in absence of AP generation.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology experiments showing PSP responses under different pharmacological conditions (Figure 1H).

claim: RSC inputs onto V1 ChCs are monosynaptic.
source: These data corroborate the idea that RSC inputs onto V1 ChCs are monosynaptic (Cruikshank et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on the TTX/4-AP experiment results (Figure 1H) which is a standard method for confirming monosynaptic connections, as established in the cited literature.

claim: Repeated optogenetic stimulation (20 Hz) of RSC inputs resulted in synaptic depression.
source: Repeated optogenetic stimulation (20 Hz) resulted in synaptic depression (Figure 1I), indicating RSC synapses may have a high release probability (Zucker and Regehr, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology experiments showing decreased PSP amplitudes with repeated stimulation (Figure 1I).

claim: RSC synapses may have a high release probability.
source: Repeated optogenetic stimulation (20 Hz) resulted in synaptic depression (Figure 1I), indicating RSC synapses may have a high release probability (Zucker and Regehr, 2002).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of synaptic depression, which is typically associated with high release probability according to the cited literature.

claim: Inducing APs in ChCs generated postsynaptic responses in ~45% (5/11) of PyCs.
source: Inducing APs in ChCs generated postsynaptic responses in ~45% (5/11) of PyCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by paired whole-cell recordings showing postsynaptic responses in PyCs when ChCs were stimulated (Figure 1K).

claim: None of the 11 ChCs responded to local PyC stimulation.
source: However, none of the 11 ChCs we recorded from responded to local PyC stimulation (Figure 1J–K), indicating a highly non-reciprocal connectivity motif.
evidence: The claim is supported by paired whole-cell recordings showing no responses in ChCs when PyCs were stimulated (Figure 1K).

claim: The connectivity between ChCs and PyCs indicates a highly non-reciprocal connectivity motif.
source: However, none of the 11 ChCs we recorded from responded to local PyC stimulation (Figure 1J–K), indicating a highly non-reciprocal connectivity motif.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ChCs innervate PyCs but PyCs do not innervate ChCs (Figure 1K).

claim: Only few if any local L2/3 PyCs provide synaptic input to ChCs.
source: It also indicated that only few if any local L2/3 PyCs provide synaptic input to ChCs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the paired recording results showing no PyC to ChC connections (Figure 1K).

claim: The rabies-labeled L1–4 neurons providing monosynaptic input to ChCs may include many inhibitory neurons.
source: These findings suggest that the rabies-labeled L1–4 neurons providing monosynaptic input to ChCs may include many inhibitory neurons, in line with previous work showing that V1 ChCs receive local input from L2/3 SST+ interneurons as well as neurogliaform cells (L2/3 NGCs), but not from L2/3 PyCs (Jiang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the paired recording results and morphological observations, and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: V1 ChCs receive local input from L2/3 SST+ interneurons as well as neurogliaform cells (L2/3 NGCs), but not from L2/3 PyCs.
source: These findings suggest that the rabies-labeled L1–4 neurons providing monosynaptic input to ChCs may include many inhibitory neurons, in line with previous work showing that V1 ChCs receive local input from L2/3 SST+ interneurons as well as neurogliaform cells (L2/3 NGCs), but not from L2/3 PyCs (Jiang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on previous published work.

claim: ChCs in V1 receive substantial input from local L5 PyCs, inhibitory neurons and long-range sources, while they locally innervate L2/3 PyCs.
source: Taken together, these results show that ChCs in V1 receive substantial input from local L5 PyCs, inhibitory neurons and long-range sources, while they locally innervate L2/3 PyCs.
evidence: The claim summarizes the connectivity findings from rabies tracing (Figure 1C), optogenetic experiments (Figure 1H), and paired recordings (Figure 1K).

claim: ChCs were mostly active during states of high arousal, more so than L2/3 PyCs.
source: In line with earlier work, correlation analysis between calcium activity and both running speed and pupil size revealed that ChCs were mostly active during states of high arousal, more so than L2/3 PyCs (Figure 2B–C, multilevel statistical analyses were performed using a linear mixed effects model [LMEM] to account for dependencies in the data and variance between mice, see Materials and methods) (Schneider-Mizell et al., 2021; Bugeon et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data showing higher correlations of ChC activity with running speed and pupil size compared to PyCs (Figure 2B-C), consistent with previous literature.

claim: ChCs within the same field of view were highly correlated with each other, much more so than L2/3 PyCs.
source: In addition, ChCs within the same field of view were highly correlated with each other, much more so than L2/3 PyCs (Figure 2B–C), suggesting that ChCs distribute a synchronized signal during high arousal.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data showing higher within-cell-type correlations for ChCs compared to PyCs (Figure 2C).

claim: ChCs distribute a synchronized signal during high arousal.
source: In addition, ChCs within the same field of view were highly correlated with each other, much more so than L2/3 PyCs (Figure 2B–C), suggesting that ChCs distribute a synchronized signal during high arousal.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the high correlation between ChCs and their correlation with arousal markers (Figure 2B-C).

claim: Both ChCs and L2/3 PyCs had strong visual responses to moving oriented gratings.
source: Although both ChCs and L2/3 PyCs had strong visual responses, ChCs were weakly tuned and showed a lower orientation selectivity index (OSI) than L2/3 PyCs (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data showing responses to moving gratings (Figure 2D-E).

claim: ChCs were weakly tuned and showed a lower orientation selectivity index (OSI) than L2/3 PyCs.
source: Although both ChCs and L2/3 PyCs had strong visual responses, ChCs were weakly tuned and showed a lower orientation selectivity index (OSI) than L2/3 PyCs (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of orientation tuning showing lower OSI for ChCs (Figure 2G).

claim: The direction selectivity index (DSI) was similar between ChCs and L2/3 PyCs.
source: The direction selectivity index (DSI) was similar between cell types.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of direction tuning (Figure 2G).

claim: ChCs responded strongly to natural images, comparable to L2/3 PyCs and L5 PyCs.
source: ChCs responded strongly to natural images, comparable to L2/3 PyCs and L5 PyCs (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data showing response strength to natural images (Figure 3B).

claim: L2/3 PyCs and L5 PyCs responded strongly to only a few images, indicating high selectivity.
source: L2/3 PyCs and L5 PyCs responded strongly to only a few images, indicating high selectivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of responses to repeated images showing steep ranked distributions for PyCs (Figure 3C).

claim: ChCs were weakly selective as shown by their strong responses to many images.
source: In contrast, ChCs were weakly selective as shown by their strong responses to many images.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of responses to repeated images showing flat ranked distributions for ChCs (Figure 3C).

claim: ChCs had significantly lower sparsity than L2/3 PyCs and L5 PyCs.
source: As evident from their flattened curve in the ranked distribution, ChCs had significantly lower sparsity than L2/3 PyCs and L5 PyCs (Figure 3C, inset).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of sparsity showing lower values for ChCs (Figure 3C inset).

claim: Correlations between ChCs were considerably higher than those for L2/3 PyCs and L5 PyCs during exposure to variable visual input.
source: Next, we reasoned that if ChCs are weakly selective for visual stimuli, their between-cell correlation should remain high even during exposure to variable visual input. Indeed, correlations between ChCs were considerably higher than those for L2/3 PyCs and L5 PyCs (Figure 3D), similarly to the situation during spontaneous behavior (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis during natural image presentation (Figure 3D).

claim: Decoding accuracy of ChCs was significantly lower than that of L2/3 PyCs.
source: Decoding accuracy of ChCs was significantly lower than that of L2/3 PyCs (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by linear discriminant analysis showing lower decoding accuracy for ChCs compared to subsampled PyCs (Figure 3E).

claim: MEIs of L2/3 PyCs often displayed clearly oriented edge-like patterns with sharp ON and OFF regions, which were much less apparent in ChCs.
source: Inspection of the MEIs and quantification of predicted responses to simple artificial stimuli revealed striking differences between cell types. For instance, MEIs of L2/3 PyCs often displayed clearly oriented edge-like patterns with sharp ON and OFF regions, which were much less apparent in ChCs (Figure 3F), while L5 PyCs showed a mixed form of selectivity, including both edge-like patterns as well as more complex textures.
evidence: The claim is supported by visual inspection and analysis of MEIs generated by the CNN model (Figure 3F).

claim: L5 PyCs showed a mixed form of selectivity, including both edge-like patterns as well as more complex textures.
source: Inspection of the MEIs and quantification of predicted responses to simple artificial stimuli revealed striking differences between cell types. For instance, MEIs of L2/3 PyCs often displayed clearly oriented edge-like patterns with sharp ON and OFF regions, which were much less apparent in ChCs (Figure 3F), while L5 PyCs showed a mixed form of selectivity, including both edge-like patterns as well as more complex textures.
evidence: The claim is supported by visual inspection and analysis of MEIs generated by the CNN model (Figure 3F).

claim: ChCs had lower OSIs than L2/3 PyCs and L5 PyCs based on CNN modeling.
source: In line with this observation and in agreement with our orientation tuning experiments (Figure 2D–E), the modeled ChCs had lower OSIs than L2/3 PyCs and L5 PyCs (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by CNN model predictions of orientation selectivity (Figure 3G).

claim: ChCs were less contrast tuned than L2/3 PyCs and L5 PyCs.
source: Accordingly, the quantification of contrast tuning and SF of modeled neurons revealed that ChCs were less contrast tuned than L2/3 PyCs and L5 PyCs (Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) and preferred lower SFs than L5 PyCs (Figure 3I), which might be related to the interdependence between contrast sensitivity and SFs (Heimel et al., 2010; Boynton et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by CNN model predictions of contrast sensitivity (Figure 3H).

claim: ChCs preferred lower SFs than L5 PyCs.
source: Accordingly, the quantification of contrast tuning and SF of modeled neurons revealed that ChCs were less contrast tuned than L2/3 PyCs and L5 PyCs (Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) and preferred lower SFs than L5 PyCs (Figure 3I), which might be related to the interdependence between contrast sensitivity and SFs (Heimel et al., 2010; Boynton et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by CNN model predictions of spatial frequency tuning (Figure 3I).

claim: The preference for lower SFs in ChCs might be related to the interdependence between contrast sensitivity and SFs.
source: Accordingly, the quantification of contrast tuning and SF of modeled neurons revealed that ChCs were less contrast tuned than L2/3 PyCs and L5 PyCs (Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) and preferred lower SFs than L5 PyCs (Figure 3I), which might be related to the interdependence between contrast sensitivity and SFs (Heimel et al., 2010; Boynton et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on known relationships between contrast and spatial frequency from the cited literature.

claim: ChCs had larger RFs than L2/3 PyCs.
source: The smooth and featureless MEIs of ChCs were further reflected by their larger RFs (Figure 3J).
evidence: The claim is supported by CNN model predictions of receptive field size (Figure 3J).

claim: ChC MEIs could be the result of combinations of L5 PyC inputs.
source: Finally, given that ChCs receive most of their inputs from local L5 PyCs (Figure 1C), we asked whether ChC MEIs could be the result of combinations of L5 PyC inputs. We generated MEIs to maximize the response of combinations of L5 PyCs and found that many of the resulting MEIs were less structured and lacked clearly oriented edge-like patterns (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational analysis showing that MEIs optimized for combinations of L5 PyCs resemble ChC MEIs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).

claim: The similarity of MEIs from L5 PyC combinations with ChC MEIs is in line with the idea that ChCs are driven by input from large number of L5 PyCs.
source: The similarity of these MEIs with those we found for ChCs is in line with the idea that ChCs are driven by input from large number of L5 PyCs (but does not exclude alternative explanations).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the similarity between MEIs optimized for L5 PyC combinations and ChC MEIs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).

claim: ChCs are visually responsive but mostly invariant to the spatial and featural arrangement of visual stimuli.
source: Together with the observation that the activity of ChCs is strongly influenced by non-visual factors such as arousal, these results support a view in which ChCs are visually responsive but mostly invariant to the spatial and featural arrangement of visual stimuli.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple observations: ChCs respond to visual stimuli (Figure 2, 3) but have low selectivity (Figure 3C, G-J) and are strongly modulated by arousal (Figure 2C).

claim: ChCs were highly active at the onset of the visual section of the tunnel but became suppressed when the visual stimuli became visible to the mice.
source: ChCs were highly active at the onset of the visual section of the tunnel but became suppressed when the visual stimuli became visible to the mice (Figure 4C–D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data in the virtual tunnel showing ChC activity patterns (Figure 4C-D).

claim: A large subpopulation of PyCs showed a similar activity profile as ChCs, suggesting functionally separate populations of PyCs.
source: Interestingly, while a large subpopulation of PyCs were activated by the visual stimuli, many others showed a similar activity profile as ChCs, suggesting functionally separate populations of PyCs (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of distinct activity patterns in PyCs during the tunnel task (Figure 4C).

claim: Hierarchical clustering revealed two clusters of PyCs with opposite activity patterns.
source: Examination of the two clusters of PyCs revealed that they had opposite activity patterns. Cluster 1 was activated by visual stimuli but suppressed in the non-visual section, while cluster 2 was suppressed by visual stimuli but activated in the non-visual section, like ChCs (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis of PyC activity in the tunnel (Figure 4C-D).

claim: Cluster 1 PyCs were activated by visual stimuli but suppressed in the non-visual section.
source: Examination of the two clusters of PyCs revealed that they had opposite activity patterns. Cluster 1 was activated by visual stimuli but suppressed in the non-visual section, while cluster 2 was suppressed by visual stimuli but activated in the non-visual section, like ChCs (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of clustered PyC activity (Figure 4C-D).

claim: Cluster 2 PyCs were suppressed by visual stimuli but activated in the non-visual section, like ChCs.
source: Examination of the two clusters of PyCs revealed that they had opposite activity patterns. Cluster 1 was activated by visual stimuli but suppressed in the non-visual section, while cluster 2 was suppressed by visual stimuli but activated in the non-visual section, like ChCs (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of clustered PyC activity (Figure 4C-D).

claim: The separability between V-PyCs and NV-PyCs was higher than expected by chance.
source: The separability between V-PyCs and NV-PyCs was higher than expected by chance (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F), indicating that V-PyCs and NV-PyCs are functionally separate clusters in our tunnel paradigm.
evidence: The claim is supported by permutation testing showing the real cluster separability exceeded chance levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).

claim: V-PyCs and NV-PyCs are functionally separate clusters in the tunnel paradigm.
source: The separability between V-PyCs and NV-PyCs was higher than expected by chance (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F), indicating that V-PyCs and NV-PyCs are functionally separate clusters in our tunnel paradigm.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the statistical analysis showing significant cluster separability (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).

claim: NV-PyCs displayed stronger responses to visuomotor mismatch compared to V-PyCs.
source: NV-PyCs displayed stronger responses to both the visuomotor mismatch and the onset of running compared to the V-PyCs (Figure 4E–F, I–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data showing differential responses to visuomotor mismatch between PyC clusters (Figure 4E, I).

claim: NV-PyCs displayed stronger responses to the onset of running compared to V-PyCs.
source: NV-PyCs displayed stronger responses to both the visuomotor mismatch and the onset of running compared to the V-PyCs (Figure 4E–F, I–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data showing differential responses to locomotion onset between PyC clusters (Figure 4F, J).

claim: Different populations of PyCs in L2/3 exist, one primarily responding to visual stimuli and the other to locomotion and visuomotor mismatch.
source: These findings support the idea that different populations of PyCs in L2/3 exist, one primarily responding to visual stimuli and the other to locomotion and visuomotor mismatch.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the clustering analysis and differential responses of V-PyCs and NV-PyCs (Figure 4).

claim: ChCs were active at the start of the tunnel, while the visual stimuli in the tunnel suppressed their activity.
source: ChCs showed a similar but more pronounced activity pattern compared to NV-PyCs: they were active at the start of the tunnel, while the visual stimuli in the tunnel suppressed their activity (Figure 4C, D, G, and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data in the virtual tunnel (Figure 4C, D, G, H).

claim: ChCs were mostly driven by locomotion.
source: Like NV-PyCs, ChCs were mostly driven by locomotion (Figure 4F) and showed strong responses to visuomotor mismatch (Figure 4E, I).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data showing ChC responses to locomotion onset (Figure 4F).

claim: ChCs showed strong responses to visuomotor mismatch.
source: Like NV-PyCs, ChCs were mostly driven by locomotion (Figure 4F) and showed strong responses to visuomotor mismatch (Figure 4E, I).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data showing ChC responses to visuomotor mismatch (Figure 4E, I).

claim: ChCs were more strongly correlated with NV-PyCs than with V-PyCs.
source: In line with this, we found that ChCs were more strongly correlated with NV-PyCs than with V-PyCs (Figure 4K).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis between ChCs and PyC subtypes (Figure 4K).

claim: PV+ ChCs showed identical activity patterns as Vipr2-ChCs.
source: We found that PV+-ChCs showed identical activity patterns as Vipr2-ChCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H–P).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data from Vipr2-Cre X PV-FlpO mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H-P).

claim: Responses to sudden halts in visual flow that were independent of locomotion were much weaker than responses to closed loop visuomotor mismatch.
source: This revealed that responses to sudden halts in visual flow that were independent of locomotion were much weaker than responses to closed loop visuomotor mismatch (Figure 4—figure supplement 1Q).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of ChC responses in open loop vs closed loop conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1Q).

claim: Open loop onset of visual flow when the mouse was not running resulted in a suppression of ChC activity.
source: In addition, open loop onset of visual flow when the mouse was not running resulted in a suppression of ChC activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1Q).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data in open loop conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1Q).

claim: In mice trained in the virtual tunnel paradigm, ChCs responded predominantly to locomotion and visuomotor mismatch when visual flow stopped during running, while they were suppressed by visual stimuli or when visual flow started while mice were stationary.
source: We conclude that in mice trained in our virtual tunnel paradigm, ChCs responded predominantly to locomotion and visuomotor mismatch when visual flow stopped during running, while they were suppressed by visual stimuli or when visual flow started while mice were stationary.
evidence: The claim summarizes the findings from the virtual tunnel experiments (Figure 4).

claim: The observed suppression of ChCs by visual stimulation in the tunnel was caused by experience-dependent plasticity induced by the repeated exposure to visual stimulation during training.
source: We therefore hypothesized that the observed suppression of ChCs by visual stimulation in the tunnel was caused by experience-dependent plasticity induced by the repeated exposure to visual stimulation during training.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis proposed to explain the discrepancy between ChC responses in naive vs trained mice.

claim: In naive mice, both PyCs and ChCs responded strongly to visual stimulation.
source: In naive mice, both PyCs and ChCs responded strongly to visual stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data showing visual responses before training (Figure 5B-D).

claim: The same ChCs showed weak or even suppressed visual responses after mice had been trained in the tunnel.
source: Interestingly, the same ChCs showed weak or even suppressed visual responses after mice had been trained in the tunnel (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by chronic calcium imaging data showing reduced ChC responses after training (Figure 5A-D).

claim: The response strength of PyCs was only mildly and statistically non-significantly reduced after training.
source: In contrast, the response strength of PyCs was only mildly and statistically non-significantly reduced after training (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by chronic calcium imaging data showing minimal changes in PyC responses after training (Figure 5D).

claim: The OSI and DSI were unchanged after training.
source: The OSI and DSI were unchanged after training (PyC OSI: p=0.1316, PyC DSI: p=0.9573, ChC OSI: p=0.2199, ChC DSI: p=0.9774, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of orientation and direction tuning before and after training.

claim: Visuomotor experience in the virtual tunnel significantly reduced responses in NV-PyCs.
source: This confirmed that visuomotor experience in the virtual tunnel significantly reduced responses in NV-PyCs (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by chronic calcium imaging data showing reduced NV-PyC responses after training (Figure 5E-G).

claim: Pairwise correlations of ChCs activity were lower in mice trained in the virtual tunnel.
source: Finally, as recent work showed that motor learning reduced correlated activity of ChCs in PFC (Jung et al., 2023), we tested whether visual experience had a similar effect in V1. Indeed, pairwise correlations of ChCs activity were also lower in mice trained in the virtual tunnel (R=0.54 ± 0.01 in naïve mice, R=0.46 ± 0.03 in trained mice, p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis comparing naive and trained mice, consistent with previous literature in PFC.

claim: ChC responses underwent sensory-evoked plasticity during the repeated visual exposure, even though the visual stimuli were different from those encountered during training in the virtual tunnel.
source: These results indicate that ChC responses underwent sensory-evoked plasticity during the repeated visual exposure, even though the visual stimuli were different from those encountered during training in the virtual tunnel.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ChCs showed reduced responses to gratings after training in a tunnel with different visual stimuli (Figure 5).

claim: The sensory-evoked plasticity of ChCs is in line with the observation that ChCs are weakly selective to visual stimuli.
source: This is in line with our observation that ChCs are weakly selective to visual stimuli.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combination of weak selectivity (Figure 3) and generalized plasticity (Figure 5).

claim: Prolonged chemogenetic activation of ChCs or PyCs results in plasticity of ChC bouton numbers at the AIS.
source: Previous work has shown that prolonged chemogenetic activation of ChCs or PyCs results in plasticity of ChC bouton numbers at the AIS (Pan-Vazquez et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is based on previous published work.

claim: PyC activation causes geometric plasticity of the AIS location and/or length.
source: In addition, PyC activation also causes geometric plasticity of the AIS location and/or length (Kuba et al., 2010; Jamann et al., 2021; Grubb and Burrone, 2010; Gutzmann et al., 2014; Wefelmeyer et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on previous published work.

claim: The average number of virally labeled ChC boutons per AIS remained constant (~2–3 ChC boutons/AIS) after training.
source: While the average number of virally labeled ChC boutons per AIS remained constant (~2–3 ChC boutons/AIS, Figure 6B and C), we observed that visuomotor experience increased the fraction of AISs being contacted by ChCs (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification (Figure 6B-C).

claim: Visuomotor experience increased the fraction of AISs being contacted by ChCs.
source: While the average number of virally labeled ChC boutons per AIS remained constant (~2–3 ChC boutons/AIS, Figure 6B and C), we observed that visuomotor experience increased the fraction of AISs being contacted by ChCs (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification showing increased fraction of contacted AISs (Figure 6D).

claim: The AIS of PyCs in trained mice were shorter than in naive mice.
source: We also found that the AIS of PyCs in trained mice were shorter than in naive mice (Figure 6E–F), resulting in an increased density of ChC boutons (i.e. ChC boutons per µm AIS length, Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification showing decreased AIS length (Figure 6E-F).

claim: Training resulted in an increased density of ChC boutons.
source: We also found that the AIS of PyCs in trained mice were shorter than in naive mice (Figure 6E–F), resulting in an increased density of ChC boutons (i.e. ChC boutons per µm AIS length, Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification (Figure 6G).

claim: ChC boutons were localized more closely to the base of the AIS after training.
source: Finally, we found that ChC boutons were localized more closely to the base of the AIS (Figure 6H–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification showing proximal shift of bouton location (Figure 6H-I).

claim: After training in the visuomotor task, response properties of ChCs in V1 had changed.
source: Taken together, these results show that after the mice were trained in the visuomotor task, not only response properties of ChCs in V1 had changed, but the number of AISs with putative ChC contacts had increased and activity-dependent AIS shortening of their post-synaptic PyC targets took place (Figure 6J).
evidence: The claim summarizes the findings from chronic imaging experiments (Figure 5).

claim: After training in the visuomotor task, the number of AISs with putative ChC contacts had increased.
source: Taken together, these results show that after the mice were trained in the visuomotor task, not only response properties of ChCs in V1 had changed, but the number of AISs with putative ChC contacts had increased and activity-dependent AIS shortening of their post-synaptic PyC targets took place (Figure 6J).
evidence: The claim summarizes the findings from immunohistochemistry experiments (Figure 6D).

claim: After training in the visuomotor task, activity-dependent AIS shortening of post-synaptic PyC targets took place.
source: Taken together, these results show that after the mice were trained in the visuomotor task, not only response properties of ChCs in V1 had changed, but the number of AISs with putative ChC contacts had increased and activity-dependent AIS shortening of their post-synaptic PyC targets took place (Figure 6J).
evidence: The claim summarizes the findings from immunohistochemistry experiments (Figure 6E-F).

claim: Recent work in adult mice has reported inhibitory effects of ChCs in prelimbic cortex, S1, and hippocampus.
source: However, recent work in adult mice has reported inhibitory effects in prelimbic cortex, S1, and hippocampus (Pan-Vazquez et al., 2020; Lu et al., 2017; Dudok et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on previous published work.

claim: ChC activity was strongly and significantly reduced after SalB injection.
source: Surprisingly, L2/3 PyCs showed only a mild increase in activity after SalB injection, even though ChC activity was strongly and significantly reduced (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by chemogenetic silencing experiments showing reduced ChC activity after KORD activation (Figure 7B).

claim: L2/3 PyCs showed only a mild increase in activity after SalB injection.
source: Surprisingly, L2/3 PyCs showed only a mild increase in activity after SalB injection, even though ChC activity was strongly and significantly reduced (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by chemogenetic silencing experiments showing small changes in PyC activity (Figure 7B).

claim: The intercept but not the slope of the locomotion modulation fit was increased for PyCs after ChC silencing.
source: Although the locomotion modulation curve of ChCs decreased in both amplitude and steepness after SalB injection, only the amplitude was affected for PyCs. Indeed, a linear fit of activity as a function of locomotion speed before and after SalB injection confirmed that the intercept but not the slope of the fit was increased for PyCs (Figure 7D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of locomotion modulation showing changes in intercept but not slope for PyCs (Figure 7D-E).

claim: Significantly more neurons increased their activity after SalB injection than in the control group (KORD: 21%, control: 13%).
source: Significantly more neurons increased their activity after SalB injection than in the control group (KORD: 21%, control: 13%, χ2-test p<0.001), while in contrast fewer neurons decreased their activity (KORD: 7%, control: 11%, χ2-test p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell analysis of activity changes after ChC silencing (Figure 7F, L).

claim: Fewer neurons decreased their activity after SalB injection than in the control group (KORD: 7%, control: 11%).
source: Significantly more neurons increased their activity after SalB injection than in the control group (KORD: 21%, control: 13%, χ2-test p<0.001), while in contrast fewer neurons decreased their activity (KORD: 7%, control: 11%, χ2-test p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell analysis of activity changes after ChC silencing (Figure 7F, L).

claim: ChCs do not differentially target PyCs based on locomotion modulation.
source: Finally, to test whether the effect of silencing ChCs preferentially affected PyCs that were weakly or strongly modulated by locomotion, we correlated the locomotion modulation index (LMI) for each PyC with the change in ∆F/F due to ChC silencing (after minus before). The correlation was weak and not significant (r=0.0068, p=0.7827), showing that ChCs do not differentially target PyCs based on locomotion modulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis showing no relationship between LMI and ChC silencing effects.

claim: ChCs only weakly modulate PyC activity, affecting only a relatively small population of cells.
source: In contrast to the idea that ChCs exert powerful control over AP generation, these results suggest that ChCs only weakly modulate PyC activity, affecting only a relatively small population of cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the chemogenetic silencing results showing only 21% of PyCs increased activity (Figure 7).

claim: The connectivity pattern of ChCs in V1 appears to be non-reciprocal.
source: Taken together, the connectivity pattern of ChCs in V1 thus appears to be non-reciprocal, as is also observed in prelimbic cortex (Lu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the paired recording results (Figure 1K) and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: Each ChC receives input from many L5 PyCs.
source: Although ChCs in V1 are sparse and the number of starter ChCs in our rabies tracing experiments was relatively low, we found large numbers of L5 PyCs providing monosynaptic input to them. This means that each ChC receives input from many L5 PyCs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rabies tracing results showing many L5 PyCs labeled relative to few starter ChCs (Figure 1C).

claim: Convergence of L5 PyC inputs, if not strongly organized, could explain the low selectivity of ChC responses to natural images.
source: This convergence of L5 PyC inputs, if not strongly organized, could explain the low selectivity of ChC responses we observed to natural images compared to those of L2/3 and L5 PyCs.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism to explain the observed low selectivity of ChCs (Figure 3).

claim: Combined inputs from L5 PyCs with diverse tuning properties are expected to result in tuning to low SFs, large RFs, and low orientation tuning, matching the modeled ChCs.
source: Combined inputs from L5 PyCs with diverse tuning properties are also expected to result in tuning to low SFs, large RFs, and low orientation tuning, matching the modeled ChCs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the connectivity pattern and the observed response properties of ChCs (Figure 3).

claim: Modeled ChCs displayed weak contrast tuning as an expected consequence of the preference for low SFs.
source: Finally, modeled ChCs also displayed weak contrast tuning. This is an expected consequence of the preference for low SFs, as these require lower contrast to be detected (Heimel et al., 2010; Boynton et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed SF preference and known relationships between SF and contrast from the cited literature.

claim: During visuomotor behavior, intratelencephalic (IT) L5 PyCs respond in a similar fashion as ChCs in that they respond to running and visuomotor mismatch but are suppressed by unexpected visual flow.
source: Interestingly, recent evidence shows that during visuomotor behavior, intratelencephalic (IT) L5 PyCs respond in a similar fashion as ChCs in that they respond to running and visuomotor mismatch but are suppressed by unexpected visual flow (Heindorf and Keller, 2022).
evidence: The claim is based on previous published work.

claim: ChCs were previously shown to display arousal-related activity in various brain regions.
source: ChCs were previously shown to display arousal-related activity in various brain regions (Schneider-Mizell et al., 2021; Dudok et al., 2021; Bugeon et al., 2022; Bienvenu et al., 2012; Massi et al., 2012), which matches our observation that their activity is highly correlated with running and pupil size.
evidence: The claim is based on previous published work and is consistent with the current findings.

claim: The neuromodulator acetylcholine is involved in axonal arborization of developing ChCs.
source: In addition, the neuromodulator acetylcholine is involved in axonal arborization of developing ChCs, further underlining the relationship between ChCs and arousal (Steinecke et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is based on previous published work.

claim: Visuomotor mismatch induces strong noradrenergic input to V1.
source: In line with this idea, it was recently shown that visuomotor mismatch induces strong noradrenergic input to V1 (Jordan and Keller, 2023).
evidence: The claim is based on previous published work.

claim: Noradrenergic input has been shown to depolarize ChCs in frontal cortex.
source: Noradrenergic input has been shown to depolarize ChCs in frontal cortex (Kawaguchi and Shindou, 1998).
evidence: The claim is based on previous published work.

claim: In V1, L2/3 PyCs respond to mismatches between visual flow and locomotion.
source: Previous work has shown that in V1, L2/3 PyCs indeed respond to mismatches between visual flow and locomotion (Attinger et al., 2017; Jordan and Keller, 2020; Keller et al., 2012; Zmarz and Keller, 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on previous published work.

claim: Two genetically defined subpopulations of L2/3 PyCs preferentially respond to (unexpected) visual stimuli or visuomotor mismatch.
source: Recent evidence suggests that two genetically defined subpopulations of L2/3 PyCs preferentially respond to (unexpected) visual stimuli, which could be considered positive prediction errors, or visuomotor mismatch, which could be seen as negative prediction errors (O'Toole et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is based on previous published work.

claim: ChCs may not be well suited for computing positive prediction errors because they only mildly inhibited L2/3 PyCs.
source: As ChCs receive input from L5 and higher-order cortical regions, they might contribute to calculating positive prediction errors by subtracting the internal representation (i.e. the predicted stimulus) from the actual visual input. However, as ChCs only mildly inhibited L2/3 PyCs, they may not be well suited for this function.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the weak inhibitory effects observed in chemogenetic experiments (Figure 7).

claim: It seems unlikely that ChCs contain high-dimensional prediction error information given that they are highly correlated in their activity.
source: Moreover, given that we and others (Schneider-Mizell et al., 2021; Dudok et al., 2021; Jung et al., 2023) have found that ChCs are highly correlated in their activity, it seems unlikely that they contain high-dimensional prediction error information.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the high correlation between ChCs (Figure 2C, 3D) and previous literature.

claim: Plasticity in predictive coding requires a gating signal that is provided by noradrenergic input.
source: Predictive coding also involves updating of the internal representation based on prediction errors. Recent evidence suggests that this plasticity requires a gating signal that is provided by noradrenergic input (Jordan and Keller, 2023).
evidence: The claim is based on previous published work.

claim: ChCs may encode arousal and play a role in the regulation of plasticity.
source: One option is therefore that ChCs also encode arousal and play a role in the regulation of plasticity.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the arousal-related activity of ChCs and their structural plasticity.

claim: Visuomotor experience in the virtual tunnel resulted in modifications in the density distribution of ChC boutons on PyC AISs.
source: This is in agreement with previous studies revealing modifications in the density distribution of ChC boutons on PyC AISs in premotor cortex upon motor learning, and in S1 upon chemogenetically activating L2/3 PyCs (Pan-Vazquez et al., 2020; Jung et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by the current findings (Figure 6) and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: Changes in ChC innervation may alter the excitability of PyCs by reducing AP generation.
source: Changes in ChC innervation may alter the excitability of PyCs by reducing AP generation.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a potential mechanism for how ChC innervation changes could affect PyCs.

claim: In vivo chemogenetic silencing of ChCs only mildly increased L2/3 PyC activity.
source: Considering our observation that in vivo chemogenetic silencing of ChCs only mildly increased L2/3 PyC activity, their electrical contribution to vetoing AP output seems, if anything, limited and affects only a small proportion of cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by chemogenetic silencing experiments (Figure 7).

claim: The electrical contribution of ChCs to vetoing AP output seems limited and affects only a small proportion of cells.
source: Considering our observation that in vivo chemogenetic silencing of ChCs only mildly increased L2/3 PyC activity, their electrical contribution to vetoing AP output seems, if anything, limited and affects only a small proportion of cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the chemogenetic silencing results (Figure 7).

claim: The findings are in contrast with the general notion that ChCs exert powerful control over PyC output.
source: These findings are thus in contrast with the general notion that ChCs exert powerful control over PyC output (Jung et al., 2022; Gallo et al., 2020), but consistent with computational simulations predicting a relatively small inhibitory effect of GABAergic innervation of the AIS, possibly involving shunting inhibition (Douglas and Martin, 1990; Shang et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with previous literature and computational models.

claim: The findings are consistent with computational simulations predicting a relatively small inhibitory effect of GABAergic innervation of the AIS, possibly involving shunting inhibition.
source: These findings are thus in contrast with the general notion that ChCs exert powerful control over PyC output (Jung et al., 2022; Gallo et al., 2020), but consistent with computational simulations predicting a relatively small inhibitory effect of GABAergic innervation of the AIS, possibly involving shunting inhibition (Douglas and Martin, 1990; Shang et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with computational models from the cited literature.

claim: Only a smaller fraction of PyCs with high numbers of AIS synapses may be inhibited when ChCs are active.
source: One explanation for the weak effects we observed is the high variability in the number of GABAergic boutons that PyCs receive at their AISs. Possibly, only a smaller fraction of PyCs with high numbers of AIS synapses are inhibited when ChCs are active.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing an explanation for the weak effects observed.

claim: Only a small fraction of PyCs increased their activity upon chemogenetic silencing of ChCs.
source: Indeed, we find that only a small fraction of PyCs increased their activity upon chemogenetic silencing of ChCs, in line with findings by others showing that manipulating ChC activity in vivo has relatively weak effects on small populations of PyCs (Lu et al., 2017; Dudok et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by chemogenetic silencing experiments (Figure 7F) and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: Manipulating ChC activity in vivo has relatively weak effects on small populations of PyCs.
source: Indeed, we find that only a small fraction of PyCs increased their activity upon chemogenetic silencing of ChCs, in line with findings by others showing that manipulating ChC activity in vivo has relatively weak effects on small populations of PyCs (Lu et al., 2017; Dudok et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on previous published work.

claim: Increasing L2/3 PyC activity decreased AIS length.
source: Increasing L2/3 PyC activity, like visuomotor experience, also decreased AIS length (Jamann et al., 2021), which is known to reduce PyC excitability (Jamann et al., 2021) and likely represents a homeostatic plasticity mechanism.
evidence: The claim is based on previous published work.

claim: AIS shortening is known to reduce PyC excitability and likely represents a homeostatic plasticity mechanism.
source: Increasing L2/3 PyC activity, like visuomotor experience, also decreased AIS length (Jamann et al., 2021), which is known to reduce PyC excitability (Jamann et al., 2021) and likely represents a homeostatic plasticity mechanism.
evidence: The claim is based on previous published work and general knowledge about homeostatic plasticity.

claim: ChC boutons face postsynaptic sites where cisternal organelles are located with micrometer precision.
source: Interestingly, ChC boutons face postsynaptic sites where cisternal organelles are located with micrometer precision (Schneider-Mizell et al., 2021; Benedeczky et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is based on previous published work.

claim: Cisternal organelles are implicated in calcium signaling and AIS plasticity.
source: As cisternal organelles are implicated in calcium signaling and AIS plasticity (Schlüter et al., 2017), ChCs may thus effectively influence these events.
evidence: The claim is based on previous published work.

claim: ChC activation could prevent homeostatic AIS shortening of L2/3 PyCs if their activity occurs during behaviorally relevant, arousal-inducing events.
source: In this scenario, ChC activation could prevent homeostatic AIS shortening of L2/3 PyCs if their activity occurs during behaviorally relevant, arousal-inducing events.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a potential mechanism for ChC function.

claim: ChC activity is primarily driven by arousal-inducing events such as unexpected visual stimuli, visuomotor mismatch, and locomotion.
source: In conclusion, our comprehensive study of the function and connectivity of ChCs in V1 reveals that ChC activity is primarily driven by arousal-inducing events such as unexpected visual stimuli, visuomotor mismatch, and locomotion.
evidence: The claim summarizes the findings from the imaging experiments (Figure 2, 4).

claim: Remarkable plasticity of ChC responses by visuomotor experience was observed.
source: We also observed remarkable plasticity of ChC responses by visuomotor experience, as well as in their innervation of the AIS.
evidence: The claim summarizes the findings from chronic imaging experiments (Figure 5).

claim: Remarkable plasticity in ChC innervation of the AIS was observed.
source: We also observed remarkable plasticity of ChC responses by visuomotor experience, as well as in their innervation of the AIS.
evidence: The claim summarizes the findings from immunohistochemistry experiments (Figure 6).

claim: In vivo, ChCs do not exert strong control over AP generation at the AIS, but only provide a weak inhibitory influence on PyC activity.
source: Interestingly, our results indicate that in vivo, ChCs do not exert strong control over AP generation at the AIS, but only provide a weak inhibitory influence on PyC activity.
evidence: The claim summarizes the findings from chemogenetic silencing experiments (Figure 7).
